Part Reader

Pick an instrument and the key signature on its part (or in the score) and get the concert key, how far every note moves, which clefs to expect, and the scale drawn as written and as it sounds.

Tell the page what is in front of you, and it tells you how to read it. The lessons behind it start at Alto and Tenor Clefs.

Your part

How to read it

Written and sounding

The sounding staff is at its real octave, so a big transposition (tuba, double bass, glockenspiel) shows ledger lines that the written part was made to avoid. That is the point of the octave transposition.

Works Cited

For students

“Transposing Instrument.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposing_instrument. Concert-pitch scores (Prokofiev), horn bass clef ambiguity, crooks, brass-band trombone in B♭.

For teachers

Adler, Samuel. The Study of Orchestration. 4th ed., W. W. Norton, 2016. Instrument ranges, clefs and transpositions.

Gould, Elaine. Behind Bars: The Definitive Guide to Music Notation. Faber Music, 2011. Grace notes, trills and other ornaments in modern notation.
